text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish newspapers this morning.

- U.S. professor Barry Eichengreen, an adviser to Finland's government-appointed committee studying the pros and cons of EMU, says planned stability and growth pact will pose big problems for EMU countries, particularly in the first years.
- Investors and analysts have started to assess human resources in their valuation of companies.
- Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's girlfriend Paivi Hertzberg became Finland's fourth lady by protocol last week when she stood at Lipponen's side at a dinner hosted by him.
- Still burdened by Soviet-era loans, the Government Guarantee Fund made a loss of over one billion markka in 1996.
- Cooperative banks have won market share from Merita among small and medium sized companies, twice-yearly survey shows.
- Swedish Wallenberg-controlled investment fund Scandinavian Equity Partners to enter the Finnish market.
- The Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK) celebrating 90th anniversary says the balance of its victories and defeats is positive.

- Nokia is a leading high-tech company since it listens to its customers, but the company should be careful not to rest on its layers and enjoy its successes, says professor Karl Moore, one of Nokia's advisers.
- Merita continues to seek ways into the insurance business, and has even considered setting up a non-life insurance company of its own.

- A merger between Pohjola and Skandia would be the next step in cooperation beteen the two, but it should only be taken after careful consideration of economic realities, says Skandia managing director Lars-Eric Pettersson.
- Legal experts reject the idea of a referendum about EMU since Finland has committed itself the single currency when it joined the EU, but the people could be heard on the timetable.
- Central Union of Agricultural Producers and Forest Owners (MTK) opposes Finnish army's decision to buy Swedish ryecrisp bread.
